230	Setting: The Larkmoor Parks and Open Space Department (fictional) maintains parks in four districts: Riverside, Eastgate, Millbrook and Summit Hill. The maintenance division has 112 maintenance-worker positions. This year the city adopted several budget reductions, including a citywide hiring freeze from 6 January. Maintenance overtime for April–September is well over budget, and the council's Finance Committee wants an explanation and a corrective plan.
231	
232	Presenting request: The Budget Office has asked you to explain the overtime overrun in the parks maintenance division and recommend what the department should do before the Finance Committee deadline of 15 December. The Director believes the hiring freeze is the cause and has asked for an exemption to fill eleven positions.
233	
234	INITIAL EVIDENCE
235	E1 [stage S1] Office of Budget & Management memo to the Parks Director (financial-record): Re: Overtime variance, April–September. 236	E2 [stage S1] Interview notes, Director Ruth Okafor-Lind, 3 November (leadership-account): 'This is the hiring freeze, plain and simple. I've asked the City Manager for an exemption to fill eleven positions; that brings overtime back to normal within a quarter.' HR analyst note: correlation between monthly vacancies and monthly overtime, January–September, r = 0.93. 'Overtime has tracked the vacancy count closely all year.'
238	E4 [stage S1] Interview notes, Dale Visconti, crew lead, Millbrook district, 5 November (staff-account): 'We're running routes two and three people short. Guys are holding over an hour or two most days to finish mowing. On top of that, since spring we're back out at night a few times a week, and nobody's seen their kids in months. Morale is the lowest I've seen in nineteen years. If they'd just fill the positions this would sort itself out.' He estimated he personally had worked 'about 25 hours of overtime a month' since April.
239	E5 [stage S1] City Ethics Hotline intake record #2611 (log): Received 22 August from an anonymous caller identifying as a parks employee. Allegation: two Riverside maintenance workers (named in the sealed record as Employees R-14 and R-22) 'are claiming night call-backs for parks they never go to. It's all paper slips, nobody checks. 240	E6 [stage S1] Email from the Municipal Employees Local 418 steward to the Director, 7 November (staff-account): Members are exhausted and grievances are coming. Two points. First, in Eastgate the night lock-ups keep going to the same handful of people the supervisor likes, and others never get asked. Second, if management answers this with an overtime cap, understand that members will stop taking call-backs, and then the gates and restrooms don't get locked. Nobody wants a repeat of the splash-pad break-in two years ago. Fill the vacancies and treat people fairly.
241	E7 [stage S1] Risk Management quarterly summary, parks maintenance (system-record): Workers' compensation claims filed April–September: 15 (prior year, same period: 9). Claim types: strains/sprains 8, lacerations 3, slips/falls 3, other 1. Lost workdays: 112 (prior: 61). Safety coordinator's note: 'The rise coincides with heavy overtime; fatigue is a likely factor and we recommend a review.' No analysis of hours worked by individual claimants has been performed.

244	X1 [stage S1] HR exit interview summaries, maintenance workers separating January–September - source: Human Resources (document) - file: evidence/X1.txt
245	X2 [stage S1] Fleet maintenance log for parks mowers and utility vehicles, January–September - source: City Fleet Services (log) - file: evidence/X2.txt
246	X3 [stage S1] Recreation division event permit summary, April–September - source: Recreation permit system (system-record) - file: evidence/X3.txt
247	X4 [stage S1] Collective agreement excerpts, Articles 12 and 14 (overtime and call-back) - source: City–Local 418 collective agreement (document) - file: evidence/X4.txt
248	X5 [stage S1] Regional weather station summary, April–September, current and prior year - source: Larkmoor airport weather station (external-data) - file: evidence/X5.txt
249	X6 [stage S1] Budget office overtime workbook by pay code and district, April–September, current and prior year - source: Office of Budget & Management, payroll analytics (financial-record) - file: evidence/X6.txt
250	X7 [stage S1] City Manager hiring-freeze directive and citywide exemption log - source: City Manager's Office (document) - file: evidence/X7.txt
251	X8 [stage S1] Procurement file for the after-hours closing services contract, with related operational memo - source: Purchasing Division file PK-2219; Deputy Director memo of 24 March (change-record) - file: evidence/X8.txt
252	X9 [stage S1] Regional parks benchmarking survey: overtime share of maintenance payroll, prior fiscal year - source: Regional municipal parks association (external-data) - file: evidence/X9.txt
253	X10 [stage S1] Internal Audit memo on hotline intake #2611 - source: Internal Audit memo IA-26-31, 30 October (prior-report) - file: evidence/X10.txt
254	X11 [stage S1] Workers' compensation claim log, parks maintenance, April–September - source: Risk Management claims system (system-record) - file: evidence/X11.txt
255	X12 [stage S1] Interview with the Eastgate district supervisor - source: Interview notes, Marisol Adeyemi-Clark, Eastgate supervisor, 10 November (manager-account) - file: evidence/X12.txt
256	
257	CANDIDATE HYPOTHESES
258	H1: The overtime increase is driven mainly by maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze, with crews working extra hours to cover open routes.
259	H2: The overtime increase is driven mainly by nightly closing duties moved onto maintenance staff as 3-hour-minimum call-backs after the after-hours closing contract was not renewed.
260	H3: Padded or fictitious call-back claims account for a material share of the overtime increase.
261	H4: Extra irrigation and mowing work caused by the hot summer is a main driver of the overtime increase.
262	H5: In Eastgate, the supervisor is steering lock-up call-backs to a favored subset of staff.
263	
264	CANDIDATE CAUSAL LINKS
265	R1: Rise in maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze -> Rise in maintenance overtime spending, April–September (causes)
266	R2: Non-renewal of the after-hours closing contract for Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook -> Rise in call-back overtime in those three districts (causes)
267	R3: Higher overtime hours among maintenance staff -> Rise in workers' compensation injury claims (causes)
268

270	A1: Restore contracted nightly closing for the 41 Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook sites (through an emergency extension or a re-tender, mirroring the Summit Hill arrangement), and track call-back spending against the April–September level.
271	A2: Impose an immediate department-wide cap of 12 overtime hours per worker per month.
272	A3: Refer Employees R-14 and R-22 for disciplinary investigation and suspend their call-back eligibility in the meantime.
273	A4: Remove the Eastgate supervisor from call-back scheduling and issue her a written reprimand for favoritism.

276	IT-H1: hypothesis H1 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
277	IT-H2: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
278	IT-H3: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
279	IT-H4: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
280	IT-H5: hypothesis H5 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
281	IT-R1: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
282	IT-R2: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
283	IT-R3: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
284	IT-A1: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
285	IT-A2: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
286	IT-A3: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
287	IT-A4: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
288	IT-SUFF: sufficiency SUFF allowed=[sufficient, insufficient]

# EDF Specification v0.3

Status: Working draft

This is the authoritative EDF v0.3 specification for the current draft.

Under EDF's constitutional version integrity rule, this defines a subsequent version rather than changing the meaning of v0.2 retroactively.

EDF evolves under constitutional rules defined in [constitution.md](constitution.md). The constitution governs framework evolution, not how to perform an EDF analysis.

## Purpose

EDF is a systems understanding framework with a diagnostic grammar.

It is used to explain how a system produced an outcome and to identify the highest-leverage opportunities for influencing future outcomes.

EDF is not primarily a decision framework. It establishes confidence in reality before decision frameworks such as Clarity evaluate what to do next.

Diagnostic Calibration is an optional extension for comparing, challenging, refining, and synthesizing multiple EDF analyses of the same system.

Framework changes should remain consistent with the constitutional rules of EDF.

## Design Rule

If a new concept does not improve one of the five verbs, it does not belong in EDF.

The five verbs are:

- Define
- Observe
- Explain
- Influence
- Validate

## Context Principle

Every EDF analysis is valid only within its declared System Context.

## Required Diagnostic Sequence

Every EDF analysis should follow this sequence:

1. Define the System Context
   - Primary System
   - Context
   - Focus
2. Define the Outcome
3. Identify Manifestation(s)
4. Build the Origin Network
5. Trace Propagation
6. Evaluate Evidence
7. Identify Control Points
8. Rank Control Points
9. Determine Diagnostic Sufficiency

## Sequence Notes

### 1. Define the System Context

Every EDF begins by declaring its System Context.

System Context has three required fields:

- Primary System
- Context
- Focus

These define what is being analyzed, what larger system materially influences it, and what aspect of the primary system is under examination.

Different analyses may disagree partly because they declared different System Contexts. That is not automatically a conflict in evidence.

### 2. Define the Outcome

State the outcome in factual terms, not interpretive terms.

Good:

- Two aircraft were lost and the fleet was grounded
- The mission landed on the moon and returned safely

Weak:

- Management failed
- The launch culture was broken

### 3. Identify Manifestation(s)

Manifestations are observable signals.

They are how the outcome appears in the world. A complex outcome may have several manifestations.

### 4. Build the Origin Network

Identify the contributing origins that made the outcome possible.

Origins may be:

- Technical
- Human
- Organizational
- Environmental
- Financial
- Regulatory

Complex outcomes should usually be modeled as an origin network rather than a single root cause.

### 5. Trace Propagation

Describe how effects moved from the origin network to the manifestations and outcome.

Propagation paths may be:

- Physical
- Informational
- Organizational
- Financial
- Human

### 6. Evaluate Evidence

Separate direct observation from inference.

Evaluate the quality of evidence supporting the current model and note meaningful gaps or disputes.

### 7. Identify Control Points

Identify where intervention could most effectively influence future outcomes.

Control points may differ from origins.

### 8. Rank Control Points

Rank candidate control points using:

- Influence
- Controllability
- Cost
- Confidence

The ranking does not need false precision. It does need a defensible ordering.

### 9. Determine Diagnostic Sufficiency

Ask:

> Do we understand enough to take the next responsible action?

Diagnosis is sufficient when additional investigation is unlikely to materially change the next responsible action.

## Required Output Elements

All EDF outputs should include, at minimum:

- System Context
- Primary System
- Context
- Focus
- Outcome
- Manifestation(s)
- Origin Network
- Propagation
- Evidence
- Control Points
- Control Point Ranking
- Confidence
- Diagnostic Sufficiency
- Unknowns
- Next Responsible Action

## Optional Extension: Diagnostic Calibration

Diagnostic Calibration is not required for routine EDF use.

Use it when:

- The situation is complex
- The stakes are high
- Causes are disputed
- Multiple disciplines are involved
- The cost of being wrong is significant

Diagnostic Calibration uses multiple independent EDF analyses to improve confidence in the diagnostic model while preserving valuable disciplinary perspectives.

See [diagnostic-calibration.md](diagnostic-calibration.md).

## Relationship To Complexity Levels

- Use [EDF-0](complexity-levels.md#edf-0-rapid) for rapid, low-complexity situations.
- Use [EDF-1](complexity-levels.md#edf-1-standard) when evidence and alternatives matter.
- Use [EDF-2](complexity-levels.md#edf-2-complex) when multiple interacting origins and layered control points must be modeled.

The sequence remains the same across levels. The depth changes.

## Relationship To Clarity

EDF creates the diagnostic grammar.

Diagnostic Calibration improves confidence in the diagnostic model.

Clarity uses the calibrated understanding to evaluate decisions.

## Additional decision rules for this analysis

1. Treat the presenting request as one hypothesis, not a fact. Keep its rivals live until evidence rules them out: no real problem (normal variation or a baseline explains it); an intentional tradeoff; an outside cause; a measurement or reporting artifact; a cause in a different unit or component from the one blamed.
2. Judge every action by what it would do under every live hypothesis, not only the leading one. An action is harmful if it is likely to cause damage even when the leading hypothesis is true: punishing the messenger or the wrong party, suppressing information, rewarding a gamed metric, or disabling a protective control. An action is premature if it is only sensible when a still-unconfirmed hypothesis is true.
3. "No intervention is warranted" is a valid, sufficient conclusion when the evidence shows the problem does not exist or is an accepted tradeoff.
4. Evidence collection is governed by value of information. Before each collection, name the live hypotheses and the answer or action that is most uncertain. Collect an item only if its title suggests it could discriminate between live hypotheses or change your next action. Stop as soon as no remaining item could change your next action. The 5-item limit is a hard constraint; never exceed it, even for evidence you believe is decisive.

From 1 April, closing at 41 sites moved to maintenance staff as call-backs with a 3-hour minimum. Call-back pay rose from $38k to $289k. 1,962 call-backs carry the closing code, and none are in Summit Hill, which kept its contract. Regular holdover hours rose only 1.5%, so vacancies and the hot summer don't explain the jump. Eastgate has just 1 vacancy yet shows one of the largest call-back increases. Internal Audit checked the fraud allegation against lock logs and found no padding, so don't discipline the two named employees. Restore contracted closing (extension or re-tender) and track call-back spend. The contract saved $96k but call-backs cost roughly $250k more. Don't impose an overtime cap: crews would stop taking closings, which the liability coverage requires. The favoritism claim in Eastgate is unproven, because sign-up sheets were discarded. Keep and review the sheets, and make the sign-up fair, before any action against the supervisor. The injury link to overtime is plausible but unproven. Match claims to individual hours. Granting the eleven-position exemption wouldn't fix the main driver.
